title: Association Rules
tagline: People who buy X also tend to buy Y. Finding those patterns automatically.
what_it_is: Association rule mining finds co-occurrence patterns in transactional data. Given a set of transactions, it identifies which items frequently appear together and produces rules like 'if a customer buys bread and butter, they also tend to buy jam.' The classic algorithm is Apriori.
key_points: Support: how often an itemset appears in the dataset. Support({bread, jam}) = fraction of transactions containing both.
Confidence: given X was bought, how often is Y also bought. Confidence(bread → jam) = support({bread, jam}) / support({bread}).
Lift: how much more likely Y is given X, compared to Y's baseline rate. Lift > 1 means X and Y co-occur more than by chance.
A rule with high confidence but low lift might just reflect that Y is extremely common — not a useful pattern.
The Apriori algorithm prunes the search space by noting that if an itemset is rare, all its supersets will also be rare.
why_it_exists: You can't manually check every possible combination of products in a store with thousands of items. Association rule mining automates the search for non-obvious co-occurrence patterns across millions of transactions. It turns raw transaction logs into actionable patterns.

breakdown.means: Number of transactions containing both X and Y
Fraction of transactions with both X and Y
How often Y appears given X
How often Y appears in general — the baseline

when_to_use: Market basket analysis — finding what products to bundle, cross-sell, or place near each other.
Recommendation systems — 'users who did X also did Y'.
Medical research — finding which symptoms or treatments co-occur.
Web analytics — which pages are viewed together in the same session.
common_mistakes: Looking only at confidence and ignoring lift. High confidence on a very common item is meaningless.
Setting minimum support too low — you end up with millions of rules including a lot of noise.
Treating correlation as causation. Bread and jam appearing together doesn't mean buying bread causes someone to buy jam.
notes: Apriori can be slow on large datasets because of multiple passes over the data. FP-Growth is a faster alternative that avoids candidate generation.
Association rules are symmetric in discovery but asymmetric in interpretation. The rule bread → jam is different from jam → bread even if support is the same.
ds_usage: Used in e-commerce for product recommendations and store layout decisions. Also shows up in fraud detection (which transaction patterns appear together) and in clinical data mining (which diagnoses or medications co-occur).
